analysis.one_liner: Protects insured patients from surprise out-of-network medical bills.
analysis.headline: A House committee approved the bill 32–13, but it never received a House floor vote and died when the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill stops the practice of "surprise billing," where an insured patient gets emergency care or scheduled care at an in-network hospital and later receives a large bill from an out-of-network doctor or facility the patient did not choose. It caps what the patient pays at the in-network amount, sets what the plan pays the out-of-network provider based on the median rate the plan pays in-network providers in the area, and creates an arbitration process for bills of $750 or more [S2]. It applies the same protections to emergency room care, non-emergency care at in-network hospitals, and helicopter or airplane medical transport [S4].
analysis.who_benefits: Insured patients who need emergency care, are treated at an in-network hospital by an out-of-network physician, or need air ambulance transport. They would no longer owe more than the in-network copay or deductible for care they could not choose in advance, and their payments count toward in-network deductibles and out-of-pocket maximums [S4].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Insured patients needing emergency or hospital care

how_it_helps.text: Emergency care is covered without prior authorization at in-network cost-sharing, no matter which provider or facility treats the patient [S4].

If an out-of-network provider treats a patient at an in-network hospital, surgical center, or outpatient department, the patient pays only the in-network cost-sharing amount and the plan pays the provider the rest of the recognized amount [S4].

The recognized amount is the median in-network rate the plan pays in the region, adjusted for inflation, with an independent dispute-resolution process available for services with a median contracted rate of $750 or more [S2].
Air ambulance rides by nonparticipating providers are treated like in-network services for patient cost-sharing, addressing one of the largest sources of surprise bills [S4].

analysis.who_pays: Out-of-network emergency physicians, hospital-based specialists, and air ambulance operators lose the ability to bill patients and insurers above the median in-network rate. Health plans and insurers pay the out-of-network providers directly, a cost they may pass to employers and enrollees through premiums.

drawbacks.text: The benchmark is frozen at each plan's January 2019 median contracted rate plus inflation, which providers argued could underpay physicians in higher-cost regions and shrink the revenue that keeps emergency and specialty coverage available in some areas [S4].
The dispute-resolution process is limited to services with a median contracted rate of $750 or more, leaving smaller disputed bills to the audit and complaint process [S2].
Because plans pay out-of-network providers directly at set rates, some of the cost could show up as higher premiums for all enrollees rather than as bills to individual patients [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade-off is straightforward: patients stop owing large bills for care they did not choose, while providers lose the ability to charge above the median in-network rate. The rate freeze at 2019 levels plus inflation is the weakest design feature, since it may not track actual local costs, but for patients the protection addresses a real and well-documented financial harm.

outcome.mechanism: It cleared the House Education and Labor Committee but was never brought up for a vote by the full House, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2021 [S6].

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 7, 2020 by Rep. Bobby Scott, chair of the Education and Labor Committee, with Rep. Virginia Foxx, the committee's top Republican, as its only cosponsor, and was referred to four committees [S1][S5][S6].
The Education and Labor Committee marked up the bill on February 11, 2020 and ordered it reported as amended by a 32–13 vote [S6].
The committee formally reported the bill as amended on December 2, 2020 [S3][S6].
No further action followed; the bill never reached the House floor and expired when the 116th Congress ended [S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Providers whose business model depends on billing out-of-network above negotiated rates — including private-equity-backed emergency physician staffing firms and air ambulance operators — kept that revenue, and insured patients went on facing surprise bills until Congress enacted a separate surprise-billing law weeks later as part of a year-end spending package.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Out-of-network providers kept billing; patients kept owing

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored jointly by the Democratic committee chair and the committee's top Republican, but the 32–13 markup vote shows real committee-level opposition; the record does not show which party the 13 no votes came from.

industries.note: The bill gives plans a predictable, formula-based payment (the median in-network rate) to out-of-network providers and shields them from balance-billing disputes, while patients get the protection. Insurers' interest and patients' interest ran together here.

industries.industry: Emergency physician staffing companies backed by private equity
industries.note: These companies profit by staying out of insurers' networks and billing patients the difference at emergency and hospital sites; the bill caps patient cost-sharing at in-network rates and pays the rest at the median in-network rate, cutting that revenue. They were among the most active opponents of benchmark-rate bills.
Out-of-network facility and physician billing at in-network hospitals would be paid at the median in-network rate rather than negotiated charges, reducing a source of high-margin revenue.
Helicopter and airplane medical transport would be treated like in-network care for patient cost-sharing, eliminating five-figure surprise transport bills to patients.
